qs.q: A 28-year-old woman at 39 weeks gestation experiences severe uterine rupture during labor, resulting in hemorrhagic shock requiring emergency laparotomy and blood transfusion. She recovers completely and is discharged home. Which maternal health category best describes this case?
o: Maternal near miss
Late maternal death
Pregnancy-related death
Direct maternal death
qs.e: A maternal near miss is defined as a woman who survived a life-threatening obstetric complication during pregnancy, childbirth, or within 42 days of termination. Direct maternal death is incorrect because the patient successfully survived the event.

qs.q: A 35-year-old woman with a history of two previous caesarean sections requests a trial of labor. Which factor most significantly increases the risk of uterine rupture during labor?
o: Ensure spontaneous onset of labor without pharmacological induction agents
Evaluate short interpregnancy interval of less than eighteen months
Assess maternal body mass index exceeding the normal reference range
Note fetal presentation in the occipito-anterior vertex position
Consider use of prostaglandins for cervical ripening or labor induction
qs.e: Prostaglandins are contraindicated in women with prior uterine scars due to high rupture risk.

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman with a history of two prior cesarean sections is in labor at 39 weeks. She requests a trial of labor after cesarean (TOLAC). Which factor most significantly increases the risk of uterine rupture during TOLAC?
o: Using prostaglandins for cervical ripening
Having maternal age over thirty-five years
Having an interpregnancy interval under eighteen months
Having a previous classical cesarean section incision
Carrying a pregnancy with a macrosomic fetus
qs.e: Classical incisions involve the upper uterine segment, carrying a much higher rupture risk than low transverse.

qs.q: A multiparous woman is diagnosed with obstructed labour. She has strong uterine contractions and a palpable Bandl’s ring. Fetal death is confirmed. The cervix is fully dilated, the fetal head is accessible, and there are no clinical signs of uterine rupture. Which definitive management is most appropriate?
o: Perform a destructive delivery using craniotomy
Perform a surgical symphysiotomy procedure
Administer an oxytocin infusion therapy
Proceed with a lower segment caesarean section
qs.e: This is advanced obstructed labour with confirmed fetal death. When the cervix is fully or nearly fully dilated, the presenting part is accessible, and uterine rupture is not suspected, a trained obstetrician may perform a destructive vaginal operation such as craniotomy to achieve delivery and avoid the added risks of caesarean section in an obstructed labour. qs.q: During induction with oxytocin, a grand‑multiparous woman suffers uterine rupture. Which factor most likely contributed?
o: Prior performance of membrane sweeping
Presence of a low Bishop score
Previous use of misoprostol for ripening
Presence of grand multiparity status
qs.e: Grand multiparity is a recognized risk factor for uterine rupture during induction. The other factors are less directly associated with rupture.

qs.q: A woman with one previous low‑transverse caesarean scar wishes to attempt a vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC). What is the approximate risk of uterine rupture with a successful VBAC?
o: Approximately 4‑9 % rupture rate
Approximately 0.5‑1 % rupture rate
Approximately 10‑12 % rupture rate
Approximately 2‑3 % rupture rate
qs.e: VBAC carries a uterine rupture risk of about 0.5‑1 %. The higher percentages refer to classical scars or are not supported by the data.

ai.title: Uterine Rupture
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: A full‑thickness tear of the uterine wall, usually in a scarred or over‑distended uterus, causing fetal and maternal compromise. Rapid recognition and surgical repair are life‑saving.

sections.p: Uterine rupture is a complete disruption of the uterine wall, often through a previous scar or over‑distension. Diagnosis is clinical, supported by fetal heart tracing and, if available, ultrasound or CT.

sections.p: Staging follows the WHO classification: Type I (incomplete), Type II (complete but uterus intact), Type III (complete with uterine rupture).

faq.q: What is the most common risk factor for uterine rupture in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Previous caesarean scar or other uterine surgery, especially when labour is prolonged or obstructed.

faq.q: Why is oxytocin avoided after a uterine rupture?
faq.a: It can increase uterine tone and worsen bleeding or re‑rupture the repaired wall.

faq.q: Can a uterine rupture be diagnosed with a bedside ultrasound?
faq.a: Yes, it can show free fluid and discontinuity of the myometrium, but clinical signs are paramount if imaging is unavailable.

exam: A woman in labour with a previous caesarean presents with sudden abdominal pain and loss of fetal station — what is your next step? — Immediate laparotomy after confirming fetal distress on CTG.
You suspect uterine rupture but the CTG is normal; what should you do? — Repeat CTG and perform bedside ultrasound; if unavailable, observe for haemodynamic changes.
A patient has a uterine rupture and is haemodynamically unstable; which drug is contraindicated? — Oxytocin, as it may worsen bleeding.
During repair, you notice a 2‑cm tear in the lower uterine segment; how do you suture? — Layer‑by‑layer interrupted sutures with non‑absorbable material.
Post‑repair, the patient develops fever and abdominal pain; what complication is likely? — Peritonitis from spillage of amniotic fluid.
A woman with a known uterine scar is in labour; what induction agent should you avoid? — High‑dose oxytocin or misoprostol without careful monitoring.
